scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4673: EMERGENCY!! The IT department is OFF THE NETWORK --
every single one of our 192.168.1.x machines, all at once, can't reach
anything!! Something around the switch box all our wires go into, switch0,
must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone look at switch0 and get us
back on the network -- the whole department is sitting here doing nothing!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The IT-segment switch is passing traffic: IT
  hosts (it_hod, it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach
  each other on 192.168.1.0/24. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of an L2 switch failure that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the IT-dept switch (switch0)
failed and took down the IT segment -- is NOT reproducible: IT hosts (it_hod,
it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach each other across
192.168.1.0/24, which means the L2 switch is passing traffic normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the IT-segment switch is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces IT host -> gateway and
host -> host pings, finds them all 0% loss (proving L2 connectivity through the
switch), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a failed switch -- declaring the
IT segment down to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The IT department's 192.168.1.x network is fully healthy. All live tests contradict the reported total outage: every IT device tested (it_hod at 192.168.1.2, it_lab1 at 192.168.1.3, it_lab2 at 192.168.1.4) successfully pings their default gateway at 192.168.1.1, reaches the CS segment (192.168.2.x), the office/principle segments (192.168.3.x, 192.168.4.x), the internet simulation segment (128.168.0.x), and the servers segment (1.0.0.x). Round-trip times are normal (sub-5 ms across campus).

Switch0, which the ticket identified as the suspect, is operating correctly. Its Linux bridge (br0) has both ports — eth0 (uplink to router0) and eth1 (downlink to lan_it) — in FORWARDING state with no errors or dropped frames. The MAC forwarding table shows router0's MAC learned on eth0 and multiple IT endpoint MACs learned on eth1, confirming normal L2 learning. There are no iptables rules or tc qdiscs on switch0 or on router0's IT-facing interface that could block traffic.

Router0 holds a complete IP routing table: directly connected 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24, and RIP-learned routes to 1.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16, 192.168.3.0/24, and 192.168.4.0/24 via router1. The RIP domain (router0, router1, router2) is converged and consistent.

Root cause: No fault exists; the network was healthy at the time of inspection and the helpdesk ticket does not correspond to any detectable network condition. No corrective action is required — the probable explanation is a transient disruption that resolved before investigation began, or a user-side issue (e.g. a single machine's ARP cache or DHCP lease) that was misattributed to switch0.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes IT hosts reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 and each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Although the agent reports successful pings to the gateway and normal RTTs, they do not explicitly state that IT hosts reached each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss at baseline.

The agent's logs show repeated successful pings from multiple IT hosts to their gateway and to remote subnets, bridge MAC learning and forwarding state on switch0, and absence of blocking iptables/tc rules; the conclusion that the IT segment and switch0 are healthy follows from those observations. Minor inference about full RIP convergence is supported by router configs and reachability tests but is not deeply probed.
